chunks.title: Low vision assessment
chunks.tldr: Low vision = function not correctable by ordinary specs/CLs (acuity, field, glare, contrast, colour, diplopia); still has useful vision — not 'blind'. US: >6 million low vision, 1 million legally blind (≤20/200 or field ≤20°); >75% over 65; AMD leading, then glaucoma, DR, cataract, optic atrophy, cornea, cortical, myopia, RP; 9% children. Start rehab early (not mid-treatment). Steps: history (tasks affected, expectations), exam undilated — re-refract (cataract myopic shift, post-trab astigmatism), ETDRS logMAR chart at 4 m / 2 m / 1 m (replaces 'count fingers'), dominant/preferred eye, Amsler binocular then monocular (dominant eye with scotoma may need occluding), contrast (Mars/Pelli-Robson) — best predictor of magnifier success; colour, glare. Near: single letters → graded continuous text.
chunks.hook: Contrast predicts magnifier success better than acuity.

cards.q: Which test best predicts response to magnification in low vision?
Why not dilate before a low-vision assessment?
cards.a: Natural pupil and accommodation are needed to assess functional performance and refraction.

chunks.title: Choosing & teaching low-vision aids
chunks.tldr: Starting add ≈ reciprocal of acuity (6/48 or 20/160 → +8 D), modified by scotoma and contrast. Try in order: spectacle magnifiers (hands free; focal distance = 1/D, e.g. 10 cm at +10 D; 4–14 D with base-in prisms binocularly, >14 D monocular), hand (4–68 D; shopping, labels; LED illumination), stand (fixed focus, good for tremor; low power allows writing), dome (hands free, limited power). Telescopes: only device focusing infinity → near; small field, shallow depth; hand-held 2–8× (signs), spectacle-mounted ≤6×. Non-optical: large print, writing/signature guides, pill organisers, liquid-level indicators, talking clocks, high-contrast marking. Tints: grey (glare), amber/yellow (contrast; block <527 nm), AR coatings, photochromics; task lighting (warm CFL/LED). Electronic: CCTV 1.5–45×, reverse contrast; portable video magnifiers; text-to-speech, phones. Train, lend devices, review in 2–3 weeks.

cards.q: Rule-of-thumb starting magnifier power for 20/200 vision?
Why add base-in prisms to high-plus reading spectacles?
cards.a: To reduce the convergence demand at the short working distance and allow binocular reading (up to ~14 D).

chunks.title: Low vision by pattern: hazy, central, peripheral
chunks.tldr: Hazy media (cornea, cataract, PCO, vitreous): reduced acuity, glare, low contrast, worse with miosis; careful refraction (pinholes, stenopeic slit), lighting, AR + grey/amber tints, UV filter, large bold print, black reading slit (magnifiers may lower contrast/glare); consider surgery — aim slightly myopic IOL for intermediate vision. Central scotoma (AMD, macular hole, myopic degeneration, optic neuropathy): reading/faces lost, mobility kept; eccentric viewing — preferred retinal locus (PRL), trained retinal locus (TRL) via OT/SLO, prism relocation; task-specific magnifiers. Peripheral loss (end-stage glaucoma, RP, PRP-treated PDR, hemianopia): reads small print but needs cane/dog; if central field <7°, magnification may overshoot field → adjustable CCTV/hand magnifier; hemianopia — saccadic scanning training.
chunks.hook: Central loss = can walk, can't read. Peripheral loss = can read, can't walk.

cards.q: What is a preferred retinal locus?
cards.a: An extrafoveal retinal area spontaneously used for fixation when the fovea is damaged (e.g. AMD).

cards.q: Why may magnification be unhelpful with a central field under 7°?
cards.a: The enlarged image overflows the tiny remaining field.
